questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Calling a generator function only creates the generator object; the body does not start. The first next() runs it up to the first yield, which is when validate is printed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first next() stops at yield. The second runs to return, giving { value: "done", done: true }, and we print its done. The third call on a finished generator gives { value: undefined, done: true }.

questions.q: Between two next() calls, what happens to a generator's local variables?
questions.explain: A paused generator keeps its whole call environment alive, like a closure does. That is what lets a generator replace the index variables of a hand-written iterator.
options: They are reset to their initial values
They keep their values: the paused call's environment is stored in the generator object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A generator object is one walk. The second spread gets a finished generator. Calling rates() again creates a new generator object that starts from the beginning.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The check is part of the generator body, so it only runs on the first next(). Put argument checks in a normal wrapper function that returns the generator if you want the error where the bad call was made.

questions.q: How do you make an object that can be walked with for...of many times, using a generator?
questions.explain: Every for...of calls [Symbol.iterator](). If that method is a generator, each call creates a new generator object, so each walk starts fresh.
options: Store one generator object on the object and return it from [Symbol.iterator]
Define the iterator method as a generator method: *[Symbol.iterator]() { … }
Generators can never be walked more than once

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Generator objects inherit from Iterator.prototype, so they have the helpers. drop(2) skips two ids, take(2) takes the next two and stops, so the infinite loop is never run to the end.

questions.q: Why is while (true) { yield delay; … } safe inside a generator, when the same loop in a normal function would hang?
questions.explain: A generator only runs when asked. The infinite loop describes an unlimited sequence; take, find, destructuring or break decide how much of it is used.
options: Generators have a built-in limit of 1,000 iterations
The generator pauses at every yield and only continues when a consumer calls next(); the consumer decides when to stop
The engine detects infinite loops in generators

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Nothing runs until the loop pulls. Then each item goes all the way through the generator to the loop body before the next item is produced.

questions.q: In the lesson's first(items, count), the count is checked right after yield item, not at the top of the loop. Why?
questions.explain: The for...of head pulls the next item before the body runs. Returning immediately after the last wanted yield stops without that extra pull, which matters when upstream stages are expensive.
options: It is just style; both versions do the same work
Checking at the top of the loop would only happen after pulling one more item from upstream, doing work (or a request) nobody needs
Because return is not allowed at the top of a loop
So that it yields one extra item

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: yield* hands out every value of any iterable, one at a time. An array gives its items; a string gives its characters.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: yield hands out one value, here the whole array. yield* delegates to the array and hands out its two items separately.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each node yields its own name, then delegates to each child in turn, which finishes its whole subtree first. That is a depth-first, pre-order walk.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The return value arrives with done: true, and spread (like for...of) stops at done: true without using its value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A yield* expression evaluates to the delegate's return value, so total collects 2 + 1. The spread finishes the outer generator (printing the total) before console.log prints the length.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first next(500) only starts the body and runs to the first yield; its argument is thrown away. next(200) makes that yield evaluate to 200, and next(300) adds 300: the total yielded is 500.

questions.q: Why is the argument of the first next() call on a generator ignored?
questions.explain: A value sent with next(value) becomes the result of the yield the generator is paused on. Before the first call, it is paused before the body, not at a yield.
options: It is a bug in JavaScript that was never fixed
At that moment the generator is not paused at any yield, so there is no expression to receive it
The first argument is used as the generator's return value
It is passed to the first console.log

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: break makes for...of call the generator's return(). The generator resumes as if a return stood at the paused yield, so its finally runs before the loop is left.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: return(value) finishes the generator at its paused yield and reports value with done: true. After that it stays finished.
options: { value: 99, done: true } { value: undefined, done: true }
{ value: 2, done: false } { value: undefined, done: true }
{ value: 99, done: false } { value: 2, done: false }
{ value: 99, done: true } { value: 2, done: false }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: throw(error) raises the error at the paused yield (the one that yielded -1). The generator's catch handles it, the loop continues, and throw() returns the next yielded value, 300.

questions.q: What happens when you call gen.throw(error) and the generator does not catch it at the paused yield?
questions.explain: An uncaught error travels out of the generator the same way it would out of a normal function, running finally blocks on the way. The generator is then completed.
options: The error is ignored and the generator continues
Any finally blocks run, the generator finishes, and the error is thrown out of the throw() call
The generator restarts from the beginning
The error is returned as { value: error, done: false }

questions.q: You call next() once on a generator that holds a lock inside try/finally, then drop the generator. What happens to the lock?
questions.explain: Nothing resumes a paused generator automatically. for...of and other consumers call return() for you; when you drive next() by hand, call return() in your own finally.
options: The finally runs immediately when the variable goes out of scope
The finally never runs; the lock is only released if someone calls return() or finishes the generator
The garbage collector runs the finally block
JavaScript throws a warning about an unfinished generator

questions.q: Why is lines.forEach((line) => { yield line.sku; }) inside a generator a SyntaxError?
questions.explain: Each function has its own body, and only a function* body may contain yield. Use a for...of loop in the generator instead of a callback.
options: yield only works directly in the generator's own body, and the arrow function is a separate, non-generator function
Arrow functions cannot take parameters in generators

questions.q: A developer stores const allOrders = paginate(fetchPage) (a generator object) at the top of a server module and loops over it in every request handler. What happens?
questions.explain: A generator object is single-use state. Create one per walk, by calling the generator function inside the handler, or expose a reusable iterable with *[Symbol.iterator]().
options: The first request uses the generator up; later requests get nothing (or the rest of a half-used walk)
Each request gets a new page
The server throws on the second request

questions.q: What does next() return on an async function* generator?
questions.explain: An async generator can await before it yields, so the result is only known later: next() returns a promise. for await...of awaits each one.
options: A { value, done } object whose value may be a promise
A promise that resolves to a { value, done } object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Async generators are lazy too. The loop stops after B, so the generator never resumes to fetch the second page.

questions.q: Why can you write for await (const chunk of fs.createReadStream("orders.csv")) in Node?
questions.explain: for await...of uses the async iteration protocol. Any object with a [Symbol.asyncIterator]() method works, and Node's readable streams have one.
options: Because for await works on any object
Node's readable streams implement Symbol.asyncIterator, so they are async iterables
Because createReadStream is an async generator function

questions.q: In the CSV export, why must a SKU like SALT,FINE be written as "SALT,FINE"?
questions.explain: In CSV the comma separates fields. A field containing a comma, a double quote or a newline is wrapped in quotes, and inner quotes are doubled.
options: Because CSV fields must always be quoted
An unquoted comma would split it into two fields and shift every later column of that row

questions.q: The export finds no orders at all. What should the CSV contain, according to the lesson?
questions.explain: A header-only file says "the export ran and found nothing". An empty file is indistinguishable from a crash, and a message in the data breaks any program that reads the CSV.

questions.q: The API throws inside paginate, three stages below exportOrders. What happens?
questions.explain: Generators do not hide errors. Each stage is resumed by the stage above it, so an error unwinds through all of them to the consumer, running every finally on the way.
options: The generator swallows the error and ends the walk quietly
The error comes out of the next() call that ran the failing code, travels up through the stages and out of the for...of, after finally blocks run
Only paginate is stopped; the other stages continue
The error is stored in value with done: true

questions.q: How does the lesson's test prove that the export streams instead of loading every page first?
questions.explain: The output text would be identical for an eager version. Only the request count differs, so that is what the test must assert.
options: By stopping early with maxRows and checking how many requests the fake API received

questions.q: Write range(start, end, step) that throws a RangeError immediately for a step of 0, and returns a reusable iterable (walking it twice gives the same numbers). Use a generator method. The end is excluded.
questions.explain: The check runs in the normal function, so it happens at the call. The generator method creates a fresh generator for every walk.

questions.q: Write a generator orderLines(orders) that yields one string "ORDER-ID SKU xQTY" per line of every order, in order. Orders with no lines produce nothing.
questions.explain: The generator pauses inside both loops at once; no index bookkeeping is needed.
questions.expected:
ORD-1 RICE-5 x2
ORD-1 OIL-1 x1
ORD-3 SALT x4

questions.q: Write an infinite generator backoff(firstMs, maxMs) that yields firstMs, then doubles each time, never above maxMs. Print the first six delays with take.
questions.explain: The generator describes the whole sequence; take(6) decides how much of it to use. The loop never ends by itself, and it does not need to.

questions.q: Write a generator flatten(value) that yields every non-array value inside nested arrays, in order, using yield* for nested arrays.
questions.explain: The base case yields a single value; the recursive case delegates to a generator for each item. An empty array yields nothing.

questions.q: Make lockedSeats print release exactly once however the walk ends, using try/finally inside the generator. The program stops the first walk early and finishes the second.
questions.explain: break calls return(), which runs the finally; a normal finish leaves the try block and runs it too. One finally covers both paths.

questions.q: Write a generator first(iterable, count) that yields at most count items and does not pull any item after the last one it needs. The source logs each item it produces.
questions.explain: Checking the count right after the yield returns before the for...of head asks the source for "C". Returning from the generator also calls return() on the source.

questions.q: Write an async generator paginate(fetchPage): it awaits fetchPage(cursor) (first cursor null), yields every item of the page, and follows nextCursor until it is null. The program prints all ids and the number of requests.
questions.explain: The do...while always fetches the first page and then follows cursors. yield* hands out the page's items one at a time; await works inside an async function*.

questions.q: Why is the generator version of "all lines of all orders" so much shorter than the hand-written iterator?
questions.explain: A hand-written next() is called fresh each time, so all state has to be kept in variables you manage. A generator keeps its whole paused call, loops included.
options: Generators run faster, so they need less code
The generator can pause in the middle of two nested loops, so the loops themselves remember the position; the hand-written next() must return after each item and store the position in index variables

questions.q: The backoff generator yields delays forever, and take(3) limits the attempts. What is the design benefit of that split?
questions.explain: The sequence describes the rule; the consumer decides how much of it to use. The same backoff can serve a job queue with ten attempts and a checkout with two.
options: It uses less memory than an array of three delays
"What the delays are" and "how many attempts to make" are separate decisions, so each can change or be tested without touching the other
Infinite generators are required by the retry protocol
It makes the retries run in parallel

questions.q: A for await...of loop walks an async generator that fetches one page per step. How are the pages fetched?
questions.explain: The generator only resumes when the loop asks for the next item. That keeps memory and load low; fetching several pages in parallel needs promise combinators and a concurrency limit, covered in later lessons.
options: All at once, in parallel, when the loop starts
One at a time: the next page is only requested after the loop body has handled the previous items
Only the first page is fetched

questions.q: In the CSV export, only exportOrders writes to the file; orderLines and toCsv only yield. Why is that split useful?
questions.explain: Keeping side effects at the edges is the same advice as for pure functions: the stages are easy to test and reuse, and the one function that touches the outside world owns the try/finally.
options: Generators are not allowed to have side effects
The yielding stages are pure transformations that can be tested with plain arrays, and cleanup lives in one place
It makes the export run in parallel
